utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, you may call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-75-PT, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Douglas Stringer appearing on behalf of the Prosecution with Muireann Dennehy and our Case Manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of Mr. Goran Hadzic is Zoran Zivanovic, lead counsel; on my right is Mr. Christopher Gosnell, co-counsel; and next to him is Mr. Toma Fila, legal consultant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I confirm with Mr. Hadzic that he can follow the proceedings in a language he understands. Thank you very much. This is the third Status Conference in this case. The purpose of this conference, pursuant to Rule 65 bis (A) is to organise exchanges between the parties as to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial. It is also to allow Mr. Hadzic the opportunity to raise any issue in relation to his mental and physical conditions while in detention. There was a Rule 65 ter Conference held this week on the 12th of June at which the parties and the legal officer of the Chamber discussed various issues related to the pre-trial preparation of the case. The Trial Chamber has been informed of what transpired at that meeting. I wish to thank the parties for their participation in that Rule 65 ter Conference. I also commend them for the spirit of co-operation that they have displayed thus far during the pre-trial preparation of the case. I acknowledge receipt of the Prosecution's Notices of Compliance in relation to access to confidential material in the Seselj case on 19 April and the Dokmanovic case on 26 April. I note that Notices of Compliance have not been filed in the Mrksic et al., Slobodan Milosevic, and Stanisic and Simatovic cases. Mr. Stringer, do you have any indication when Notices of Compliance will be filed in these three cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Once we complete the work on the Prosecution exhibit and witness lists that are due to be filed next Tuesday, we're going to redouble our efforts on the access issues, and we expect to file Notices of Compliance by mid-July at the latest for those cases. I should point out that we still don't have -- I'm informed we do not have a decision yet on access in the Milosevic case -- no, I'm sorry that's not correct. I think we have all the access decisions in. We're in the process of reviewing what's confidential and expect to file our notices by mid-July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have any comment in relation to access to confidential material?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I apologise for the interruption. I just want to indicate that a letter went across to the Defence earlier this morning from the Prosecution. At the 65 ter meeting on Tuesday, the Defence inquired whether the Prosecution was able to indicate roughly the volume of materials that we're reviewing on the remaining three access cases, and we did gather that information and send that across to counsel in a letter earlier today. A copy of the letter was sent to the Chamber's legal officer as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think I've seen a copy of that, Mr. Stringer. Thank you very much. I note that the second joint report on agreed facts has been filed. I wish to thank the parties for their timely filing of that report. I'm also very grateful for the continued progress towards -- towards reaching agreement on facts pertinent to the trial where possible. The Trial Chamber is anticipating the filing of the Prosecution's witness and exhibit lists on the 19th of June. We also anticipate on this date the notice of all protective measures from prior proceedings, motions for the variations of protective measures and any new motions for additional protective measures. Moreover the Prosecution's deadline for the disclosure of statements, transcripts and exhibits is 26 June. I acknowledge receipt of the Prosecution's 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th reports on disclosure. Would I now ask the Prosecution to report on the state of the Rule 68 disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Rule 68 disclosure is being handled as part of all of the disclosure in the case. Because of the way we're doing trial preparation here, which is to review lists of documents that are generated on database searches, we're manually going through literally hundreds of thousands of documents. That's what this exercise has entailed. And so in the course of these document reviews we're selecting documents that go on to the exhibit list, other documents that, although possibly of relevance, are not going on the exhibit list because we don't envision tendering them. And in the course of this we're also identifying anything that appears to us to fall within Rule 68, and so all of that is happening at the same time, and all of the disclosure that is taking place is -- is Rule 68 disclosure falls within that. I should also indicate that the Rule 68 -- we're keeping special track, obviously, of Rule 68 documents that come to our attention during the document reviews, and much of that will be within the disclosure of all the exhibits that takes place on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Zivanovic, any comment to make in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. At the last 65 ter Conference, issues regarding the management of evidence during the pre-trial and trial phase were discussed, in particular the state of disclosure pursuant to Rule 70. Mr. Stringer, do you have an update as to how much material is pending Rule 70 clearance and a target eventually, a target date for completion of all Rule 70 disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll address each of those. I've come today with specific figures so that the Chamber knows exactly where we stand on Rule 70. At the moment, and of course this changes as we go through the completion of the exhibit list, at the moment we have 145 exhibits on the exhibit list that fall within Rule 70 for which consent has already been granted. We've already obtained consent for the disclosure of those. Now, we have currently about 267 documents for which there are pending Rule 70 requests to different providers. A couple of those requests go back actually now two or three months ago that we made them. That figure's higher than what I indicated to the Chamber's legal officer on Tuesday, because actually I was under the impression that a couple of the older requests have been resolved. They have not been. After I began looking into this again on Tuesday, we contacted now all the providers who have pending requests. One of them wrote us back rather quickly and indicated that they were currently working on it and they expect that we would have their answer by the 26th of June. So at least in respect of probably about 50 or 60 documents, we're going to have that resolved by the 26th of June. We continue to do what we can to urge the providers of the remaining documents to process the outstanding requests. Unfortunately -- Your Honour, I'm reluctant to give a target date because I just can't control that other than to say that, again, a couple of these -- one of these requests was made more than two months ago, another one was made more than a month ago, and we are trying to follow up without being too pushy, if I can put it that way. Because the document review process has been continuing up until within the last few days, which is being used to generate the exhibit list, there are additional Rule 70 documents that are being identified for inclusion on the list for which we have not yet sought consent to disclose, and I expect that that is probably going to be in the range of about 150 documents. And as soon as the exhibit list is filed, we are going to be getting the requests out for consent in respect of those remaining documents. So those are the figures as they stand today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stringer. I understand, of course, the fact that you -- that there are factors that you don't have under control, and I trust you will keep a reasonable pressure on the issue. We all understand that obtaining clearance from all the relevant Rule 65 providers -- Rule 70 providers, sorry, is a matter of urgence so that the case can be ready to go on trial in October. Mr. Zivanovic, any comments on your part on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have no comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point, I would like to ask Mr. Hadzic whether there are any issues in relation to his case that he would like to raise today. This may include, Mr. Hadzic, issues regarding your mental or physical condition while in detention and please note that we can go into private session for these purposes, if you would prefer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I have to say that I have no comments to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other matters that the parties wish to raise today? Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I did want to make a few remarks and actually ask for the Chamber's guidance or at least to flag an issue that would assist the Prosecution in going forward in respect of 92 ter statements. So one is -- is to sort of foreshadow what's coming in the witness summaries, and then the second issue on 92 ter is more of a question that perhaps we could resolve on a going-forward basis, not necessarily today. The first issue relates to the Chamber's direction in respect of what we're calling the hybrid 92 ter witnesses, those for whom there's 92 ter evidence in the form of a statement and for whom additionally there may be testimony viva voce when they actually come to testify. At the present time on our list we have about 60, six zero, 60 witnesses whom we've categorised as 92 ter witnesses. About half of those we currently see as being strictly 92 ter with not very much, if anything, in the way of viva voce testimony and certainly staying within the 30 minutes of direct examination that the Trial Chamber has laid down in its guide-line. For the other half, again about 30, we do envision that there would be viva voce evidence, and we're very aware of the Chamber's -- what we understand to be a strong preference that witnesses when they come as 92 ter evidence witness that they do not talk about or repeat things viva voce that are already included in their 92 ter statement. And we're guided by that now as we prepare the witness summaries for the 92 ter witnesses because the Chamber's indicated that it wishes for us to indicate in the summaries what parts of the evidence would be from the statement versus what parts would be the viva voce part. And to be candid, Mr. President, the difficulty for us at the present time lies in identifying in the summaries what would be parts of the evidence that are the viva voce part, and the reason for that, if I may say, is that we expect that as we talk to witnesses, parts of their narratives, and as the trial actually develops, parts of their narratives, parts of their statements may need to be developed, in our view, beyond what is already contained in the statement, although it may be on the same topic. There maybe additional evidence, new things that witnesses say. In previous submissions that we've made to Your Honour and in the 65 ter meetings, the Prosecution's indicated that the work of re-interviewing the 92 ter witnesses, having them review their prior testimony and statements, amalgamating those statements together into a single statement when that's required, that that work remains to be done. It has not yet been done as we've worked on preparing the witness lists and the exhibit lists and the disclosure. It's during this process to come that the Prosecution envisions that it will become in a position to identify what parts of a 92 ter witness's testimony ought, in the Prosecution view, to be led viva voce. That's a long way of saying that at the present time and in all candour, Mr. President, there isn't much information in the witness summaries of these 92 ter witnesses that, as of today, we can indicate would be viva voce. And the process of reviewing the 92 ter statements of these witnesses, preparing the amalgamated statements, taking additional relevant information that would justify the viva voce evidence as hybrid testimony, because that is to come, we propose and are planning that, of course to the extent that there is supplemental witness evidence in the form of witness statements, that would be immediately disclosed to the Defence and that we could on an ongoing basis revise and update the witness summaries so that as viva voce or what we view as appropriate viva voce evidence becomes known to us and evident, we can then indicate to the Chamber and the Defence that we were proposing the witness be led viva voce on this aspect. So this is essentially just to foreshadow, if I may, that in the coming witness summaries, there's not going to be significant amounts of evidence for which we're proposing viva voce testimony. We hope that the Chamber will accept that the process will continue to develop and that there may be, as we go forward, revisions of the proposed witness summaries that will then provide a fuller view of proposed viva voce testimony of these witnesses. I hope I've said that clearly enough for Your Honour, and I stand ready to answer any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have -- I have one indeed, Mr. Stringer. On -- how did you or on what basis did you determine then that half of your witnesses are pure 92 ter and half of them are not? You must have some kind of indication for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We do. It's based upon having reviewed the witness evidence. Again, we have -- we're talking about some statements now that go back many years to the Milosevic case or testimonies from other cases, such as the Mrksic case, Stanisic/Simatovic, which is more recent. The witnesses gave evidence in that -- in those cases which, although very relevant for this case, is not -- wasn't focused directly on this accused, and there are times when in reading the statement we see that in fairness, in our view, another question needs to be asked that might bring that statement more focussed to this particular case and this particular accused. So it's actually a matter of -- of refocussing the witness, if I may put it that way, on this case, and that obviously Mr. Hadzic or the specific subject matter of this case was not foremost in the mind of the lawyer or the investigator who was taking the statement back when it was made. And so we can see that and that is something that we feel we must try to develop now in the coming weeks prior to the trial, and that is where we are as we stand. And what we are proposing is to obviously provide immediate notice to the Defence, update the summaries and to -- and so that everyone sees, to the extent there may be changes or new aspects, I shouldn't say new, but focus now of -- that relates more to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I conclude then like this: That in first summary you'll provide, there will be an indication whether this is a purely 92 ter or eventually a hybrid witness, and that as soon as you have the information on what part -- on what the subject of the viva voce part will be, that we will be informed. What we try to avoid is specifically to get at a hearing with a 92 ter witness and hear then for the first time that it will not take 30 minutes but it will take two hours because there is an important part of viva voce to cover. So if we can agree that we get the information, that there is a part viva voce and what it is about as soon as you have that information, I think that's as far as we can go. We, of course, understand that the preparation of a trial is an ongoing business.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That is absolutely the intention, Mr. President, to provide immediate notice once we have the information. And if I may say, it's -- it's our intention that that would be at the very latest six weeks, which is the Chamber's guide-line on the filing of the statement. Now, there are times when that -- I'm sure there will be times where the Prosecution applies for a change after six weeks, before the witness testifies, but we expect that six weeks is, for the most part, going to be the latest time in which we will have given the notice and identified what we are proposing to be the viva voce aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course. Nothing is certain, and even that isn't. Your second point, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The second point was to ask for guidance and this would involve input from the Defence, so I don't expect it to be resolved today. Once we file the witness and exhibit lists, a big focus of the team is going to turn toward the preparation of the 92 ter statements and the creation of amalgamated statements when it's necessary to do so. What we're finding is that for a number of witnesses, again who have testified in other cases in the past, they give evidence, that is, the relevant evidence for this case, their experience in Croatia in the relevant areas during the relevant time-frame, but we have a number of witnesses then whose experience moves off elsewhere, say, to Bosnia-Herzegovina down in 1992 or 1993 or 1995. And in some cases this accounts for a very large volume of the witness's testimony; because if the witness came and testified in the Milosevic case, that witness might have spoken a little bit about Vukovar and spoken a great deal about Sarajevo. And, on the one hand, we think that it's most efficient to delete and to not include in the 92 ter statement the testimony and the -- the testimony that relates to matters that are clearly falling outside the geographic and the temporal scope of this case; on the other hand, we're talking not only about direct examination but cross-examination, and the Prosecution is uncomfortable modifying a witness's testimony and tendering it as evidence. It may be that there are aspects of the cross-examination that relate to Sarajevo that the Defence, nonetheless, thinks goes to the witness's credibility and that it should therefore be included. So there's a bit of tension here between including what's possibly a fairly significant volume of material in a ter statement that doesn't really relate to this case, but at the same time, ensuring that all relevant aspects of the evidence, both direct and cross, are before the Trial Chamber. So we're not -- that's something I think that we could use some guidance on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I -- I see the problem, and you've probably considered -- or you could eventually consider the possibility of highlighting the parts you want to submit and then leave to the Defence eventually to add, eventually in another colour, other highlights of parts that they want to add to what you want to tender as the witness's -- as the relevant witness's statement. That seems to me a first possible solution. I'm thinking of a way, and just -- just to suggest and to put in the idea, a better of way improving the way you can handle, for instance, 200 or 250 witness statements in which you have three or four pages of different parts in the statement that you have to look at, but you can eventually think about that. But my first idea would be can we work with -- if parties agree with that, can we work with highlighted parts. But I would say let's ask the parties to consider and to discuss this amongst them and report to us what seems to be the best solution. Is that all right with both of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I then thank you kindly for your appearances today. I thank the parties for their continuing co-operation with each other and with the Chamber in getting this case ready for trial. A Scheduling Order for the next Rule 65 ter Conference and status Conference has been issued. The next 65 ter Conference will be held on Thursday, 6 September, at 2.00, and the next Status Conference will be held on Thursday, 13 of September, at 2.30 in a courtroom to be determined. This Status Conference is now adjourned.
